title: Supreme Court Holds Night-Time Vehicle Repossession Without Notice Violates Articles 14 and 21
meta_description: SC rules a financier cannot repossess a hypothecated vehicle by force or at night without the contractual notice, and directs RBI to enforce compliance.
bench: Justices Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Alok Aradhe
case_name: Hari Dutta Sharma v. State of U.P. & Ors.
body: A truck owner who watched his vehicle driven away in the middle of the night by men he did not know, only to discover later that they had been sent by his own financier, has produced a Supreme Court ruling that goes well beyond his individual case to question whether the Reserve Bank of India's recovery guidelines mean anything in practice at all. Hari Dutta Sharma had taken a commercial vehicle loan from Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company in 2019, secured by hypothecation of the truck, and the financier had already repossessed and released the vehicle once before, in 2022, after an earlier default.

In April 2023 the truck was taken again, this time at night and without the seven-day notice the loan agreement itself required before any repossession. Sharma's writ petition before the Allahabad High Court was dismissed, reportedly on grounds of delay in approaching the court, leaving him to carry the matter to the Supreme Court. A bench of Justices Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Alok Aradhe allowed his appeal, finding that the manner of repossession, not merely the underlying default, was itself unlawful.

The Court held that a night-time seizure of a hypothecated vehicle, carried out without the contractual notice period the financier's own loan agreement promised the borrower, violates Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution. A financier's right to recover security on default does not translate into a licence to use force or surprise against the borrower; the contractual right to repossess, the Court held, can only be exercised through the safeguards the agreement itself, and the RBI's fair practices guidelines, build around that right, not by sending agents to take the vehicle in the dark before the borrower has had the notice period he bargained for.

Having found the repossession itself unlawful, the Court went on to treat the RBI's regulatory framework on recovery conduct, specifically the fair practices code and the directions on the engagement and conduct of recovery agents, as carrying binding force on lenders rather than operating as aspirational guidance lenders could observe or ignore as convenient. On that basis the Court ordered Cholamandalam to close Sharma's loan account, refund the Rs 4.5 lakh the truck was sold for in August 2023 with 6% annual interest, and pay Sharma Rs 10 lakh as compensation for mental agony and loss of livelihood plus Rs 50,000 in costs, restoring him to the position he would have been in had the financier followed its own contractual and regulatory obligations.

The Court did not stop at deciding the individual dispute. It directed the Reserve Bank of India itself to take effective steps to ensure that non-banking financial companies and scheduled commercial banks actually comply with the recovery guidelines the RBI has already issued, observing that those guidelines had, in practice, existed largely on paper without any real mechanism forcing lenders to follow them on the ground. A regulator's guidelines that nobody enforces protect no one, and the Court's direction puts the burden back on the RBI to show that its own framework has teeth rather than leaving aggrieved borrowers to litigate each instance of forceful repossession individually.

For NBFCs and banks running vehicle and equipment finance books, the ruling raises the practical cost of treating repossession as a purely operational matter best left to recovery agents working outside business hours. A seven-day notice clause in a loan agreement is not boilerplate that can be skipped when a recovery agent finds it convenient to act at night; skipping it converts a contractually permitted repossession into one that attracts constitutional scrutiny, compensation, and now a court-ordered demand on the regulator to tighten supervision across the sector.

Borrowers facing repossession threats, and the lawyers advising them, now have a Supreme Court ruling squarely on point for challenging any seizure that departs from the loan agreement's own notice terms, independent of whether the underlying default itself is disputed. The judgment also gives the RBI's recovery guidelines a different legal character going forward, one closer to binding obligation than suggested practice, which lenders drafting internal recovery agent protocols would be unwise to ignore.
why_it_matters: NBFCs and banks can no longer treat repossession of hypothecated vehicles as a purely contractual or operational matter to be executed by recovery agents at their convenience; a seizure that skips the agreed notice period or occurs through force or at night now exposes the lender to a constitutional challenge and compensation, and the RBI faces a direct Supreme Court mandate to make its recovery guidelines actually enforceable rather than advisory.
card_summary: SC holds a financier's night-time, no-notice repossession of a hypothecated truck violated Articles 14 and 21, ordering loan closure, a Rs 4.5 lakh refund with interest, Rs 10 lakh compensation, and RBI enforcement.
card_tip: Before authorising a vehicle repossession, confirm the contractual notice period has run and that no agent will act by force or outside daylight hours.
verification_notes: The citation (2026 INSC 998), the bench, the 2019 loan and 2022 prior repossession, the April 2023 night-time seizure without the contractual notice period, the Allahabad High Court's dismissal, the holding that the repossession violated Articles 14 and 21, the loan-closure and refund-with-interest direction (Rs 4.5 lakh, the truck's August 2023 sale price, plus 6% annual interest), the Rs 10 lakh compensation for mental agony and loss of livelihood, the Rs 50,000 costs, and the direction to RBI to enforce compliance are corroborated across LiveLaw, LiveLaw Biz, Verdictum, Law Street, ThePrint, SupremeToday and KNN India. Sources differ on the precise decision date (16 or 17 September 2026) and on the civil appeal number; 16 September 2026, the date given by LiveLaw Biz and consistent with the Wednesday hearing reported, is used here, and the appeal number is omitted given the inconsistency across sources.
